  • Recent findings suggest that bond 4 carries a 3% target annual yield, paid in BTC weekly over a six-month term.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that registration is open for the bond starting ~Dec. 5, after Bond 3 sold out at 1,005 BTC with 21shares and Bullish.

GRAND CAYMAN, Cayman Islands, Nov. 24, 2026. Stacks Labs today announced 1,050 BTC of capacity for Bond 4 of Bitcoin staking with Stacks, a Bitcoin layer where BTC holders earn BTC. The bond starts ~Dec. 5, and institutions can register at stacks.co/institutional-bitcoin-staking.

Recent findings suggest that bond 4 carries a 3% target annual yield, paid in BTC weekly over a six-month term. Each BTC staked is paired with STX worth 5% of its value, so filling Bond 4’s 1,050 BTC of capacity requires a corresponding STX commitment. Rewards come from Stacks miners, who commit BTC through Proof of Transfer (PoX), the consensus mechanism Stacks has run since January 2021.

Every bond since the Genesis Bond launched in September has filled. 21shares returned for Bond 3, and Bullish (NYSE: BLSH) joined as the first top-10 public Bitcoin treasury company to stake BTC.

“Opening more than 1,000 BTC of fresh capacity for institutions reveals how strong the demand for Bitcoin yield has become,” noted Muneeb Ali, CEO, Stacks Labs, and founder of Stacks.

Institutions can stake from qualified custody, including BitGo. During the bootstrap phase, self-custodial Bitcoin staking is whitelisted. Holders who are not on the whitelist can take part through pooled Bitcoin staking at stacks.co/bitcoin-staking.

Stacks is a Bitcoin layer where BTC holders earn BTC. With Bitcoin staking, holders stake BTC with STX, and their BTC stays on the Bitcoin L1 under their own custody. Stacks has distributed over 4,200 BTC in rewards to participants since 2021. Learn more at stacks.co.

Media contact: Shannon Voight, PR & Events, Stacks Labs, [email protected].

Institutional onboarding: https://www.stacks.co/institutional-bitcoin-staking.

Starting in 2027, Apple TV will become the exclusive U.S. streaming home of F1 Academy, the all-female racing series developing the next generation of talent.

Industry observers note that fans will be able to watch every qualifying session and race on Apple TV, bringing more visibility to a series that is promptly gaining momentum. It also expands Apple's partnership with Formula 1, which began its five-year U.S. broadcast deal with the streaming service in 2026.

For Austrian driver Emma Felbermayr, who represents the Audi Revolut F1 team in F1 Academy, the announcement is particularly exciting.

“Apple TV is such a big platform, and it's all about F1 Academy getting more attention,” Felbermayr told Women's Health in Las Vegas ahead of the Grand Prix. “It just makes the interest into the sport much bigger, and that's what we need. We need to have more girls interested in the sport so that we get more attention. In the end, we want to get seen by people.".

Rolled out in 2022, F1 Academy is a Formula 4-level development series designed to create more opportunities for women in motorsport. And its impact extends beyond the racetrack.

At a private dinner in Las Vegas celebrating the Apple TV announcement, F1 Academy managing director Susie Wolff reflected on the series' rapid rise.

“It's incredible how the sport has shifted in the last five to seven years,” Wolff said. “Women have a huge part to play in that shift, and that has been part of the reason why F1 Academy has had so much success in the short space of time.” The dinner event, co-hosted by Wolff and F1 Chief Commercial Officer Emily Prazer, brought together women from across the worlds of sports, entertainment, and advocacy, including activist Malala Yousafzai and model Kelly Piquet.

That growth is personal for Felbermayr, who says F1 Academy has helped her become more confident both in and out of the car. Once a self-described shy person, the 19-year-old has learned to navigate interviews, limited track time, and the pressure of competing at a high level.

According to recent reports, “I got so much better in the language of English. That's maybe just a small part of it, but just getting more confident in front of the camera, but also in the car,” says Felbermayr, who just signed on for a third F1 Academy season with Audi. “Every challenge grows yourself as a person, and I think that's something I really saw in the last two years.”.

With seven race weekends on the 2027 calendar, including stops in Austin and Las Vegas, American fans will have plenty of opportunities to get acquainted with F1 Academy's rising stars. And with Apple TV bringing their races to a wider audience, more young girls will have the chance to see what's possible behind the wheel.

2027 F1 Academy CalendarMarch 19-21: Jeddah Corniche Circuit, Saudi ArabiaApril 16-18: Shanghai International Circuit, ChinaMay 21-23: Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve, CanadaJuly 2-4: Silverstone Circuit, Great BritainJuly 30-August 1: Hungaroring, HungaryOctober 22-24: Circuit of The Americas, United StatesNovember 18-20: Las Vegas Strip Circuit, United States.

Citing people familiar with the plans, the Journal reported that US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer could release the findings of a months-long investigation into manufacturing overcapacity as soon as this week.

On Nov. 24, the USTR docket still indicated the investigation opened in March and four days of hearings in May, listing no determination or tariff schedule for the case. A check of published USTR notices in the Federal Register found none dated Nov. 19 through Nov. 24.

According to recent reports, the available White House, Treasury, and Commerce trade agency listings carried no announcement of the action described in the report. Importers still have no published list of the goods that would face these duties, the rates that would apply or the date they would start.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 20, Greer told Bloomberg Television he expected the work to be finished by year-end. He declined to specify which economies might face additional tariffs.

USTR opened the investigations on March 11 under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 and is examining whether policies such as subsidies sustain more manufacturing capacity than demand supports and whether those practices burden or restrict US commerce.

According to recent reports, the agency’s fact sheet described the sectors it wanted to examine. An investigation of how a product is made or subsidized leaves open which products, if any, may face duties.

The inquiry covers 16 economies, including the EU. The March 17 initiation notice also lists Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan and India. Hearings ran from May 5 through May 8.

Under Section 304 of the Trade Act, USTR must determine whether the practices are actionable. If it makes an affirmative finding, it must decide what action, if any, to take. The law requires the trade representative to publish the determination and the facts it rests on in the Federal Register.

Industry observers note that public hearings ended in May. The USTR docket still demonstrated no determination on Nov. 24.

A USTR determination would establish whether the practices are actionable and, if so, what action USTR should take.

#190324. Muscle Size vs. Strength: Which Matters More for Living Longer? Experts Explain

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1760 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Muscle Size vs. Strength: Which Matters More for Living Longer? Experts Explain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when it comes to aging well, you've probably heard that building muscle is one of the best things you can do for your body.
  • According to recent reports, resistance training, which is often used as an umbrella term, can have different goals, including building muscle size and increasing maximal strength.
  • On the other hand, training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force your muscles can produce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when it comes to aging well, you've probably heard that building muscle is one of the best things you can do for your body. And it's true: Maintaining muscle mass is essential for staying healthy, mobile, and independent as you get older. But here's something you might not realize: Having more muscle doesn't necessarily mean you're stronger. And when it comes to living as long (and as well!) as possible, that distinction matters.

According to recent reports, resistance training, which is often used as an umbrella term, can have different goals, including building muscle size and increasing maximal strength. Training for muscle growth, known as hypertrophy training, focuses on increasing the size of your muscles, says Vonda Wright, MD, an orthopedic surgeon who researches longevity and muscle health.

On the other hand, training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force your muscles can produce. It’s often measured by how much weight you can lift in a particular exercise, Dr. Wright explains. Although larger muscles have the potential to produce more force, muscle size alone doesn’t determine strength. “That’s why someone who is smaller can sometimes be stronger than someone with visibly larger muscles,” she adds.

Meet the experts: Vonda Wright, MD, is an orthopedic surgeon and author of Unbreakable. Mark Kovacs, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, longevity and human performance specialist, and founder of the Kovacs Institute in Atlanta. Stuart Phillips, PhD, is a muscle researcher and professor of kinesiology at McMaster University. Ben Walker, CPT, is a personal trainer and founder of Anywhere Fitness in Dublin, Ireland.

Sources indicate that still, both adaptations play an important role in healthy aging—especially since muscle mass and strength naturally decline with age. Building muscle supports your joints and bones, helps regulate metabolic health, and gives you the strength and physical capacity to keep moving and stay active, indicates Mark Kovacs, PhD, CSCS, an exercise physiologist, longevity and human performance specialist, and founder of the Kovacs Institute. Strength, meanwhile, allows you to put that muscle to work, whether you’re carrying groceries, climbing stairs, or getting up from the floor, he explains.

Industry observers note that it’s imperative to build both strength and muscle for a long, healthy life. But if your goal is to stay active and independent well into your later years, one may be worth prioritizing over the other.

It has been revealed that resistance training can help you build muscle and become stronger, but these are distinct goals that emphasize different outcomes. Training for muscle growth focuses on increasing muscle size, while training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force you can produce, claims Kovacs. The two goals overlap, and people typically gain both muscle and strength through resistance training. But you can formulate your workouts to emphasize one outcome over the other, he adds.

Industry observers note that for instance, if your goal is maximal strength, the weight you lift matters more. So, training for strength means practicing movements with loads that feel heavy to you, states Stuart Phillips, PhD, a muscle researcher and professor of kinesiology at McMaster University. Strength gains depend not only on muscle size, but also on how effectively your nervous system activates your muscles and how efficiently you perform the movement. “Lighter weights can still make you stronger, but taking them to failure doesn’t automatically make them equivalent to heavier training for maximizing strength,” Phillips explains. For this goal, he recommends 2 to 3 sets of roughly 4 to 8 reps with a challenging weight, stopping before your technique breaks down.

In terms of muscle growth, both lighter and heavier weights can build muscle—what matters is that your body is sufficiently challenged. Of course, lighter weights will require more repetitions to grow muscle, Phillips states. (In fact, his research shows that performing roughly 20 to 25 repetitions with light weights produced similar muscle growth to sets of 8 to 12 repetitions with heavier weights when both were taken to failure.).

As a rule of thumb, Phillips recommends choosing a weight that makes the last few reps feel challenging while leaving about two good reps in reserve. (If you finish 25 reps and feel like you could easily do five more, the weight is probably too light to provide enough of a stimulus to spark growth.) One way to gauge this is with the resistance-training rating of perceived exertion (RPE) scale, which measures how hard a set feels based on how many more reps you think you could complete with good form, he explains. The scale runs from 1 to 10: An RPE of eight means you could squeeze out about two more reps, a 9 means you have one left, and a 10 means you’ve reached failure and can’t complete another rep.

Industry observers note that the number of sets you perform matters for building muscle, too. Doing one challenging set per exercise consistently over time can grow muscle, Phillips indicates, but research suggests that performing multiple sets generally leads to greater muscle growth.

It has been revealed that strength, which is the maximum force you can produce in a particular task, directly influences how well you can move through everyday life. “Strong muscles support our skeleton, protect our joints, improve metabolic health, and allow us to continue doing the things we love at 50, 70, and 90,” says Dr. Wright. Strength helps us with getting up off the floor, carrying our own suitcase, climbing a mountain, playing with grandchildren, and living independently long-term.

Consider something as simple as getting out of a chair. When you’re younger and stronger, Kovacs states that movement may require only a small percentage of your maximum strength. As you lose strength with age, though, that same movement requires more of what you have available. If you aren’t regularly training it, everyday activities can become increasingly difficult, he explains. But when you continue to build strength as you age, you have more to pull from, making those activities easier.

Industry observers note that additionally, research draws a direct connection between strength and a longer life: A 2026 study in JAMA Network Open looked at the association between muscular strength and mortality. Over 5,000 women ages 63 to 99 underwent testing for grip strength, chair stand performance, and a timed walk test. Participants also mailed health update questionnaires annually between 2012 and 2014 until 2023. They found that higher muscle strength was associated with lower mortality.

Strength training is also associated with cardiometabolic benefits, endurance performance, and bone density—which are all notable for living long and well. In fact, a small 2022 study in Sensors had 29 postmenopausal women with osteopenia or osteoporosis (when you have lower bone mineral density than normal) either do strength training exercises with heavy and moderately heavy weights, or no exercise at all, for six months. The group that strength trained had higher bone mineral density at the end of the trial period.

Industry observers note that muscle is one of your body’s best forms of insurance for getting older. Everyday activities depend on having enough muscle (as well as strength) to do them independently. “Muscle supports our joints and loads our bones, helping stimulate the bone-building process, but it’s also essential to mobility and functional strength," Dr. Wright explains. “If we want to continue getting ourselves off the ground, climbing stairs, carrying things, traveling, playing sports, and living independently, we need muscle to do it.”.

Research also concludes that less muscle mass is associated with a higher risk of mortality. A 2023 review in PLOS One observed 16 studies with over 81,000 participants and looked at the connection between their body composition and when they died. The review concluded that a low skeletal muscle mass index was significantly associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality.

It has been revealed that additionally, having muscle mass can improve your metabolic health. A 2025 study in Nutrition & Metabolism had older participants with type 2 diabetes either build muscle through resistance training alone, resistance training and eating a whey protein supplement, or doing neither of the two, for 12 weeks. Those who completed the muscle-building interventions significantly improved their blood glucose control and insulin resistance.

Plus, lower muscle mass is linked to poor balance and a higher risk of falls. So, maintaining muscle helps protect your mobility and independence as you age, Dr. Wright adds. A 2020 study in Menopause Review had 122 women over 60 do physical performance tests (gait speed test, grip strength, and a timed up and go). Their body composition was measured, and they filled out a survey of how often they fell in the past year. Less muscle was associated with a higher risk of falls.

A well-rounded workout plan should naturally progress both muscular size and strength. After all, they address different pieces of the same puzzle and one form of training can help you make progress in the other. As you build muscle, you generally increase the amount of tissue available to produce force, notes Ben Walker, CPT, a certified personal trainer and founder of Anywhere Fitness in Dublin, Ireland. And as you train for strength, your brain and nervous system become better at coordinating and activating those muscles, he explains.

It has been revealed that if you’re looking for a blueprint that’ll help you build both strength and muscle, check out our Women’s Health+ exclusive workout aims. Each one comes with four weeks of expert-programmed workouts, science-backed nutrition advice, and evidence-based recovery methods.

It has been revealed that remember, longevity isn’t about simply adding years to your life. It’s about extending your healthspan, or the number of years you remain healthy, mobile, and strong. “The goal is to bring our healthspan as close to our lifespan as possible, and for me, that means building a body that can carry you through the life you want to live,” says Dr. Wright. That way, you’ll be ready to throw grandkids around at 60, deadlift hundreds of pounds at 70, and lift your own suitcase on vacation with your family in your 80s and beyond.

Coldcard Postmortem Says Weak Seeds, Not Hacked Devices, Drove Bitcoin Thefts

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coinkite on Tuesday published its full postmortem on the Coldcard seed-generation flaw that let thieves drain bitcoin from customer wallets starting in July, saying no device was hacked and that the stolen keys were rebuilt offline from weak seeds.
  • 23 and modeled on a National Transportation Safety Board accident report, lays out how the defect shipped in Coldcard firmware from March 29, 2021, through July 30, 2026, and why years of outside reviews missed it.
  • “The losses are real and, for some customers, life-changing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coinkite on Tuesday published its full postmortem on the Coldcard seed-generation flaw that let thieves drain bitcoin from customer wallets starting in July, saying no device was hacked and that the stolen keys were rebuilt offline from weak seeds.

The 18-page report, dated Nov. 23 and modeled on a National Transportation Safety Board accident report, lays out how the defect shipped in Coldcard firmware from March 29, 2021, through July 30, 2026, and why years of outside reviews missed it.

“The losses are real and, for some customers, life-changing. No report or firmware update can undo that. We are sorry,” Coinkite wrote.

A seed is the list of recovery words that controls a bitcoin wallet, and it is only as safe as the randomness used to create it. Coldcard devices were supposed to draw that randomness from the hardware random number generator built into their STM32 chip.

Instead, a firmware setting switched that hardware source off, and a safeguard in Coinkite’s libNgU code library failed to catch it. Seed generation quietly fell back to Yasmarang, a predictable software generator built into MicroPython, the programming environment the firmware runs on.

Nothing crashed, and the devices produced normal-looking seed words. Coinkite estimates affected seeds carried roughly 40 bits of effective security on the older Mk2 and Mk3 models and about 72 bits on the Mk4, Mk5 and Q, against an intended 128 bits. That shrinks the pool of possible seeds enough for attackers to search it offline.

Industry observers note that the report says Coinkite’s release checks confirmed the hardware code was present, but never confirmed that seed generation actually reached it. At least 15 independent review efforts since 2021 also missed the flaw, including two paid third-party reviews and an AI-assisted firmware review this year that produced 85 candidate findings.

Unexpected transactions from affected seeds began July 29. Coinkite said it identified the defect the next day, after users discovered thefts, and shipped fixed firmware for every supported release track on July 31.

Recent findings suggest that as of Nov. 18, Coinkite had received about 300 loss-related support tickets tied to 242 customer accounts, or about 0.21% of its estimated Coldcard user base. The manufacturer’s blog post cites 236 accounts. Because Coldcard is self-custodial, Coinkite can only count losses that customers report, and it says the true number is likely higher.

Industry observers note that the report cites Galaxy Research figures showing 1,778.84 BTC stolen from more than 8,600 addresses, worth about $107 million at today’s price. Galaxy pegged losses above $115 million in August, based on prices when the coins were taken, and white hats later moved some exposed coins into a recovery trust.

Industry observers note that who found and exploited the flaw is still unknown, and law enforcement is investigating. The report calls AI-assisted discovery “a plausible hypothesis, not an attribution,” noting that the first thefts came two days after the full model weights of the AI model Kimi K3 were released. Bitcoin Core developers ended long embargoes last month for bugs that AI tools can easily rediscover.

It has been revealed that coinkite remarked an independent review by Keylabs, published Oct. 15, found the defect “fully closed” in Mk5 firmware 5.6.2 and 5.6.3 and Q firmware 1.5.2Q and 1.5.3Q. That review did not cover Coldcard’s Edge releases, a preview track for developers and early adopters.

Newer Coldcard firmware now requires users to add their own randomness, through key presses, dice rolls or coin flips, and mixes it with three hardware sources. The device also checks at startup that seed generation reaches the hardware generator, and stops if it does not.

But a firmware patch does not repair a seed that was already created on affected firmware. Coinkite told owners whose seeds were made on affected firmware to install verified fixed firmware, create a newly introduced seed and move their coins. Seeds made with at least 50 private dice rolls were not weakened.

Recent findings suggest that three of the report’s 15 recommendations to Coinkite remain open, including whether to compensate affected customers. The organization stated it has “no decision” on a plan yet and asked whoever holds the stolen bitcoin to return it through [email protected].

These Fragrances Double As Skincare Products

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • Sources indicate that I REMEMBER being about 10 years old and spending hours in my grandmother’s product-strewn bathroom.
  • It has been revealed that I was transfixed by the ritual of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that I REMEMBER being about 10 years old and spending hours in my grandmother’s product-strewn bathroom. In the middle of her pink-tiled bathroom was a small alcove with a skirted makeup table. Perched on top were probably a dozen, maybe more, intricately detailed glass perfume bottles and coordinating scented powders. The fragranced dusting powders were applied with oversized, almost-feathery puffs to absorb oil from the skin and leave it smelling fresh and clean, while the perfume itself acted like a topper, locking in the coordinating scent.

It has been revealed that I was transfixed by the ritual of it. Scent has always had an emotional lure of sorts. Whether it transports you back in time or conjures a mood, the connections that fragrances evoke are personal and emotional. All that unfolds once a fragrance makes contact with the skin. As the notes dance and bloom, the scent really takes hold. But what if the skin-scent connection went one step further? Could a fragrance improve the tone, texture, quality, and health of our skin?

It’s no longer a theoretical—it’s reality.

Dual-purpose beauty products used to be a one-off. Nowadays, it’s expected that a product will tackle two concerns at once. “We’ve already seen growing interest in functional fragrances, scents formulated with sensitive skin in mind, and alternative fragrance formats like hair mists and body oils, so it’s not surprising to see brands exploring ways to incorporate skincare ingredients into traditional fragrance formats,” notes Darryl Do, a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. The idea of perfume that offers skincare benefits is fitting, and, quite honestly, maybe even a little late to the game. “It feels relevant as consumers become more conscious of the ingredients in their beauty products and what they intend to deliver,” Do continues.

Meet the experts: Darryl Do is a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. Jenna Queller, MD, is a dermatologist and founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton. Charlene Valledor is a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. Farah K. Ahmed is president and CEO of the fragrance creators association (FCA).

It has been revealed that as skincare and scent merges into a brand-new category, some are wondering what took so long. “Scent has long been part of wellness rituals,” indicates Farah K. Ahmed, President & CEO Fragrance Creators Association (FCA). “What’s different today is that we have science showing that functional fragrances actually work.” We spoke with scent experts and a cosmetic chemist for the backstory on the trend and how to make the most of fragrances infused with skincare so you can reap the benefits.

Skin and scent have a long-standing connection. “In the fragrance industry, the term “skin scent” describes fragrances that are close to the natural scent of skin in order to complement it rather than overpower it,” says Do. But how a scent wears on the skin varies.

According to recent reports, it’s all comes down to body chemistry, which includes pH, how much natural oil is produced by your skin, moisture and perspiration levels, and natural odor, explains Charlene Valledor, a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. That’s why the very same perfume can smell wildly different from one person to the next. Someone with a skin pH of 5.75, more sebum, or who eats a spicy diet, for example, will provide a different environment than someone with a skin pH of 4.75, drier skin, and eats virtually no spicy foods.

But it doesn’t stop there: What you apply to your skin before perfume also influences how a fragrance takes hold. By the time most people finish their morning routine, they’ve already created a fragrance profile and applying perfume introduces another layer on top of that existing baseline, Do states.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, your skin doesn’t always play nicely with certain scents. The ingredients in the bottle themselves, which includes everything from the concentration of alcohol to the presence of essential oils can cause itching, redness, and general irritation. “Fragrance can directly disrupt skin’s protective barrier or trigger an outright allergic reaction,” explains board-certified dermatologist Jenna Queller, MD, founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton, FL. “Irritation can happen to anyone, particularly when the skin is already dry or compromised. An allergy is different: the immune system has become sensitized to a specific ingredient.”.

Dr. Queller notes that while certain compounds like cinnamal, eugenol, isoeugenol, and geraniol are well-known contact allergens and can damage or irritate the outer layer of skin and weaken the protective barrier, others, such as limonene and linalool, which are commonly found in citrus, floral, and herbal fragrances, can become more allergenic after exposure to air. “A higher concentrations can increase the risk of irritation,” she says. “However, no single concentration guarantees a product is safe for everyone. If you develop a true allergy, even a small amount can trigger a reaction.”.

According to recent reports, deciphering how much allergen is in a perfume—even in a natural or organic scent or essential oil, which isn’t necessarily a safe option for sensitive skin—is difficult. “You can’t judge a fragrance by how strong it smells,” Dr. Queller suggests. “Subtle scents can contain allergens, which is why the ingredient list matters more than the intensity.” If your skin is sensitive or dry, or you are rosacea- or eczema-prone, a fragrance intolerance or allergy, which often manifests as redness, itching, dryness, burning, and even swelling, hives, or blisters, is likely to form more easily, especially since she notes the skin barrier may already be impaired.

In a recent development, so, what’s the best way to wear a fragrance while also safeguarding your skin’s health, especially if one of the trendier skincare-infused fragrances may not be a good fit? Dr. Queller suggests applying the scent to clothing rather than directly to the skin, although she says it’s not a guarantee because fragrance can transfer to the skin. Of course, each scents’ chemical composition can vary so naturally, a bit of trial and error may be involved to determine which irritate you specifically.

Sources indicate that the latest fragrance technology is innovative because it not only helps you avoid irritant reactions, it promises to care for a nurture skin directly. In fact, it seems we’re moving toward a world in which dual-purpose fragrances can leave you smelling good and feeling soft. It makes sense when you learn that keratinocytes—the primary cells in your epidermis—contain olfactory receptors that respond to certain fragrances, says Dr. Queller. “Skin has its own sensory biology,” she says, “and research suggests scent may influence notable cellular functions, including skin regeneration and wound healing.” In fact, one study showed that Sandalore, a sandalwood note, activates a receptor that speeds up cell growth and migration to help close cuts and sores. Another research paper found that the same pathway prolonged the growth phase of cultured human hair follicles.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a welcome development. We all live extremely busy, over-scheduled lives and most of us want beauty products that do more than one thing. The new Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume captures this ethos brilliantly. It combines plant-derived exosomes, thought to boost collagen, reduce inflammation, and support healthier-looking skin, with one of two scents: a warm blend of vanilla, amber, and almond or an oceanic mix of sheer musk, sea air notes, and driftwood. Similarly, Bella Hadid’s alcohol-free, essential oil-powered Orebella collection promises to hydrate skin with a bi-phase formula that simultaneously moisturizes while delivering a long-lasting scent. Another offering worth noting is Salt + Stone’s Body Mist. In six intoxicating scents, each light-as-air-mist is infused with glycerin and red algae for smooth, touchable skin. The idea of all of these is that rather than leaving your outer layer dehydrated and more susceptible to aging—a common complaint with scents formulated with alcohol—these products support dry skin and enhance its moisture levels.

Sources indicate that future Society’s unscented Base Scent follows a similar path in a different way. It works with the skin’s natural microbiome to help the body smell better. It relies on aspergillus ferment, zinc, and arginine, and you can wear it on its own or layer it over perfume to create a more neutral body scent over time. The microbiome also factors significantly into Argentum’s Les Perfumes Infinis collection. Water-based and free of potentially drying alcohol, each of the twelve scents is formulated in such a way as to not disrupt the delicate balance of bacteria naturally found on your outer layer.

Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume.

This fragrance, proven to last up to twelve hours, harnesses the power of plant-derived exosomes and an advanced hydration complex to hydrate skin and strengthen its barrier.

All of Orebella’s scents, including this brand-new blend of creamy milk, woody amber, and fresh bergamot features a base of hydrating snow mushroom and the brand’s signature five-oil blend.

Salt & Stone Bergamot & Hinoki Body and Hair Fragrance Mist.

Recent findings suggest that salt + Stone’s body products have rightfully gained a cult following and their hair & body mists are no different. What does make them different is that they contain humectant glycerin to help skin hang onto moisture and red algae to promote smoothness. This bergamot and hinoki blend is one of their latest.

A scent with no scent? Yup. This one is formulated with prebiotics that work with your skin’s natural microbiome to keep your natural scent more consistent and balanced.

ARgENTUM Les Parfums Infinis LOVER Eau de Parfum.

It has been revealed that each of these alcohol- and solvent-free fragrances is gentle on skin and blended based upon one of the main elements (Earth, Air, Water). Lover, for example, is a mix of geranium, rose, and berries meant to evoke a garden after a rainfall.

So, can a few spritzes of a skin-boosting fragrance achieve the same goals as a watery serum or thicker moisturizer? Potentially, but as Dr. Queller shares, it really comes down to the formulation. “A fragrance that incorporates ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, ceramides, or nourishing emollients can help improve skin hydration and support the skin barrier.” Her advice? Look beyond the label and marketing claims. “A beautifully formulated fragrance can offer skincare benefits, but that doesn’t automatically make it suitable for sensitive skin.”.

Recent findings suggest that what is undoubtedly true is that the skin-scent connection remains strong, perhaps stronger than ever, and this new fragrance category may provide more options for those who may not have been able to wear scent before. These next-generation fragrances go one step further than functional fragrances, which can boost your mood, productivity, and wellness, to focus on skin health in a way that was never tackled before. So go ahead and douse yourself in one of these new skin health-boosting fragrances and wait for everyone to ask, “What perfume are you wearing?”.

Recent findings suggest that elise Minton Tabin is an award-winning beauty journalist, editor, and expert with more than 19 years of experience. She started her career in public relations before shifting to editorial. Elise rose the ranks at NewBeauty magazine from an editorial assistant to Executive Beauty Editor, overseeing and reporting on all things beauty, plastic surgery, anti-aging, health, and wellness.

Sources indicate that brian Underwood is beauty director at Women’s Health, where he oversees content strategy for the brand across all platforms, including digital, print, and social. Anchorage Digital Sets Up Asset Manager to Offer Bitcoin Yield to Clients

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anchorage Digital, the first federally chartered crypto bank in the U.S., is moving into asset management with a new subsidiary that will offer custody clients a way to earn yield on their bitcoin.
  • Industry observers note that the unit, called 61st Parallel Asset Management, is expected to start operating by early December, CEO Nathan McCauley said in an interview to CoinDesk.
  • “We have increasingly heard clients say they want to earn on top of the assets they hold at Anchorage — something that’s very common among the large financial institutions of the world,” McCauley said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anchorage Digital, the first federally chartered crypto bank in the U.S., is moving into asset management with a new subsidiary that will offer custody clients a way to earn yield on their bitcoin.

Industry observers note that the unit, called 61st Parallel Asset Management, is expected to start operating by early December, CEO Nathan McCauley said in an interview to CoinDesk. Its first product will be a bitcoin-denominated fund, meaning returns are measured in BTC rather than dollars. The name nods to the city of Anchorage, Alaska, which sits at 61 degrees north latitude.

“We have increasingly heard clients say they want to earn on top of the assets they hold at Anchorage — something that’s very common among the large financial institutions of the world,” McCauley said.

Anchorage has filed a Form ADV, the disclosure document investment advisers use to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission or state regulators, or to report as exempt advisers. The form covers a firm’s ownership, business, assets under management, fees and conflicts of interest. As of Tuesday afternoon, the SEC’s public adviser database highlighted no record for 61st Parallel, so the filing’s details were not yet public.

The entity itself is not new. New York state records show that 61st Parallel Asset Management LLC, a Delaware firm, registered to do business in New York on July 8, listing an office on Park Avenue South in Manhattan.

In a recent development, anchorage already lets clients earn on some holdings. Its website lists staking, which pays rewards for helping secure proof-of-stake networks, and a separate rewards product for eligible assets. Bitcoin runs on proof-of-work and cannot be staked natively.

Recent findings suggest that anchorage has not noted publicly how the fund will generate yield, what it will charge or which clients will qualify. Those details matter to bitcoin holders, because bitcoin pays no interest on its own. Common ways to earn on it include lending coins out, posting them as collateral or selling options against them, and each carries its own risk.

Public companies have already tested some of those approaches. Trump Media disclosed this month that it had pledged about 73% of its bitcoin to an options program in which the counterparty can rehypothecate, or reuse, the coins.

Recent findings suggest that founded in 2017, Anchorage received a national trust bank charter from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency in January 2021, the first crypto firm to win one. The OCC lifted a 2022 consent order over the bank’s anti-money laundering controls in August 2025.

The bank no longer stands alone. Last December, the OCC granted conditional approvals to five more digital asset firms, including Circle, Ripple, BitGo, Paxos and Fidelity Digital Assets, to become national trust banks.

The asset manager is the latest in a run of expansions. On Nov. 5, Anchorage Digital Swap Dealer LLC applied to the National Futures Association to register as a swap dealer with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The company remarked much of its options growth has come from public companies holding bitcoin and ether on their balance sheets.

In a recent development, in February, Tether made a $100 million strategic investment in Anchorage at a $4.2 billion valuation, after picking Anchorage Digital Bank as the issuer of its U.S. stablecoin. Anchorage also ran its first employee tender offer at that valuation instead of raising new primary capital.

According to recent reports, in June, the firm rolled out off-exchange settlement with Binance, letting institutions trade on the exchange while their assets stay in segregated custody at the bank. Anchorage also offers trading, staking and settlement to institutional clients.

The swap dealer application remains under review by the National Futures Association, and McCauley said at the time that the organization was not in a position to speculate on timing.

I’ve Weighed the Same for 7 Years. My Body Has Changed Completely.

  • A FEW MONTHS ago, my friend Jack Espy stopped by Men’s Health HQ, and as we were talking shop and swapping stories with MH senior editor Ryan Brower about our favorite fitness-workout-wellness gear, I asked them both to name their single favorite product.
  • Jack chose his Garmin watch and raved about its amazing battery life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

A FEW MONTHS ago, my friend Jack Espy stopped by Men’s Health HQ, and as we were talking shop and swapping stories with MH senior editor Ryan Brower about our favorite fitness-workout-wellness gear, I asked them both to name their single favorite product.

Jack chose his Garmin watch and raved about its amazing battery life. Ryan named his Adidas Adizero Evo SL running shoes. As for me? It was hard: the one thing, among allll the things, that actually moves the needle? After thinking for a full 20 seconds, it finally hit me:.

Weird and kind of random, right?

According to recent reports, I thought so, too. I’ve never cared that much about how much I weigh, mostly because I didn’t have to and I didn’t want to. I’ve always been on the leaner side, so for most of my adult life, the extent of what I knew about my weight came down to whether my pants fit.

Recent findings suggest that then, about a decade ago, I started getting more serious about putting on muscle, and my trainer at the time, the major-armed and bigger-brained David Otey, introduced me to a kind of body-composition testing, a.k.a. “bioelectrical impedance analysis,” or BIA. The tech has been used to estimate body composition for decades, and you’ve probably seen one of the more sophisticated machines at your gym or doctor’s office. Step onto a platform, grab a pair of handles, wait 30 seconds, and the machine spits out a breakdown of how much of you is body fat, skeletal muscle mass, and more.

David walked me through how BIA works: The machine sends a teeny-tiny electrical current through your body. Electricity moves more easily through lean tissue than through fat, so by measuring how that current travels through you, the machine can estimate how much fat and muscle you’re carrying.

Industry observers note that in 2019, I bought an InBody Dial H20N for my bathroom. By then, BIA was well established in the consumer “smart scale” market, and InBody’s scale was among the more advanced at-home options, using sensors at both your hands and feet to take a more complete reading of your body than the foot-only models that were common at the time. The app tracks every measurement, so I can see not just what my body looks like on any given day but how it has changed over time.

To understand why I love the damn thing, it’s important to know that I weigh roughly the same today as when I first brought the scale home seven years ago.

A conventional (dumb) scale would look at seven years of strength training, workouts I wanted to skip, workouts I probably should have skipped, and a totally unreasonable amount of thought about what I put into my body and deliver its verdict: Congrats, you weigh the same!

But the InBody tells a different story. When I look back at my results from 2019, it estimated that I carried about 84 pounds of skeletal muscle mass and 33 pounds of body fat. Today, it shows I’ve got around 95 pounds of skeletal muscle and 24 pounds of body fat. Yep: According to the scale, I’ve added 11 pounds of muscle while losing about 9 pounds of fat—all while my total body weight has barely moved. (I won’t mention that I did all this during a stage of life when building muscle, and simply holding on to it, gets harder than it was when I was 25. But I will mention Men’s Health has done an amazing guide to body recomposition that is worth checking out.).

Now, a necessary reality check: Those body-comp numbers aren’t exact measurements in the same way that the number staring back at me from a dumb scale is a measurement. They’re estimates. My hydration levels can throw them off. What I just ate can throw them off. A hard workout can really throw them off.

It has been revealed that still, in studies comparing the InBody to much fancier ways of measuring body composition, the scale holds up surprisingly well for something that lives in your bathroom. There’s even a new model, the H40, that Inbody notes is even more precise. (I keep meaning to buy it, but then something breaks in my house and a new scale gets knocked down the priority list.).

Industry observers note that none of this means that I obsess over whether I have 94.7 pounds of muscle on Tuesday and 93.9 on Thursday. What makes this useful to me aren’t the exact numbers; it’s the direction they’re headed in. I still don’t really care how much I weigh—I wear the same pants size as when I was 25 and 35, and all my blood work is fine. But I’m trying to carry more muscle, less fat, and a stronger, more capable body into the second half of my life. I just want to know that some of my ass-busting efforts are paying off.

A dumb scale can’t tell me that. But a smart scale—this smart scale—is giving me all the direction I need.

FIND THE INBODY DIAL H20 ON AMAZON.

Richard Dorment is the editorial director of Men’s Health and Women’s Health.

In a recent development, there are many perks of being a Women’s Health style writer, and testing comfortable sneakers for work ranks very high on the list. My days are basically a rotation of steps—commutes, errands, long walks in the name of journalism—which means I’ve become extremely picky about what earns a spot on my feet. But time after time, I keep coming back to Hoka, aka the King of Cushion.

Since the brand released in 2009, Hoka has perfected the balance between support and comfort (the number one feature in a walking shoe), says podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM, foot surgeon and owner of Central Park Sole in New York City.

Recent findings suggest that hoka has not only asserted itself as a top contender in the sneaker scene, but the brand has also become a style statement, too, making ortho-looking shoes look cool with their plush cushioning. The brand churns out a bunch of styles for all sorts of activities, from running shoes to hiking boots, but Hoka’s walking shoes are some of my favorites. I get that combing through all the specs can get overwhelming, so luckily, I’ve done the legwork for you by testing and walking in Hoka sneaks for the past two years. Plus, I enlisted the help of Schaeffer and other WH editors to get the scoop on the right shoes for you.

According to recent reports, after testing nearly every Hoka model, the Clifton 11 reigns supreme for walking. I was also a fan of the previous Clifton 10, and the newest version feels very similar. It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning that gives me a spring in my step.

Recent findings suggest that the first major difference I noticed is how light the Clifton 11 feels. Even after wearing it for several hours at a time, it doesn’t feel bulky or clunky. Which makes sense: Hoka did shave nearly half an ounce off the weight compared to the 10. The toe box is slightly more narrow, too, but I actually preferred the more secure fit because it kept my foot from sliding around without feeling cramped. If you like a little more wiggle room for your toes, I would suggest opting for the wide sizing, though.

Despite its lighter weight, it has an ample stack of foam padding throughout the midsole. That weightless yet cushiony feel makes it ideal for my longer walks throughout NYC. The shoe has a mild heel drop (the same as the previous model at 8 mm), which helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot.

Industry observers note that I also found that the foam absorbed impact well on both pavement and the treadmill. My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never felt fatigued wearing this shoe. There's technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely notice it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running. I’m also a fan of the durable rubber outsole that gives plenty of traction. I never feel like I’m going to slip while wearing these, even when walking down slippery subway stairs.

So far, the Clifton 11—which was debuted alongside the new Clifton Pro— does a great job of keeping my feet comfy and supported. It’s a great shoe for anyone in need of a comfortable, everyday walking sneaker that can also handle the occasional jog (unlike the Clifton Pro, which is geared more toward high-speed running).

Read more: Hoka Clifton 11 and Clifton Pro Review.

Sources indicate that technically, the Mach 7 is a running shoe—but don’t let that marketing label fool you. The previous iteration, the Mach 6, took home our 2025 Fitness Award for top walking shoe thanks to its blend of responsive cushioning, breathability, and lightweight construction—and the Mach 7 has built on that winning formula with an updated outer and grippier bottom. I’ve walked more than 150 miles in the ultra-light, ridiculously comfortable sneaker, and not once have I felt even a bit of foot fatigue or soreness.

Recent findings suggest that the midsole is stiff yet flexible, while the cushioning is relatively low-key compared to its popular sibling, the Bondi 9. But, its slimness is an illusion. In fact, it’s just as supportive as most Hoka models and still offers a spring-like sensation after your foot hits the ground for a comfortable stride. This style doesn’t offer any special stability features for people whose feet tend to roll while walking, but I found it still does a decent job of keeping my feet in a neutral position, despite my high arches and tendency to underpronate (or land on the outer edge of my feet).

According to recent reports, I wear the standard size and haven’t had any issues, but Accardi prefers the wide sizing, which she finds more suitable for her bunions and ability to spread her toes. If you have similar foot concerns or just like more wiggle room, we definitely recommend the wide fit.

While our one complaint with the Mach 6 was its lack of traction, I thankfully found that the Mach 7 features a more durable rubber at the heel and a stickier rubber up front, which makes a noticeable difference in grip.

It has been revealed that thanks to its incredible support and cushioning, the Gaviota 6 keeps my feet pain-free even after miles of wear. The shoe is designed with Hoka’s signature H-frame, which is a firm, dense foam in the midsole that provides a stable base to really lock your feet in place. I recently discovered that I have high arches, causing my ankles to roll inward when I walk, so this shoe has been a game-changer for me and my recent foot woes.

In a recent development, while the Gaviota 6 is geared toward flat arches on paper, I’m right now contending with a bit of foot fatigue from my upcoming 1-mile-per-day (at least!) running goal, and the Gaviota 6 has given my dogs the TLC they need. That’s likely due to the combo of plush cushioning and stability tech. After weeks in the Gaviota 6, my gait naturally shifted from a heel strike to a midfoot strike—exactly what Schaeffer recommends for pain-free walking.

According to recent reports, other super supportive sneakers I’ve tried tend to have a stiff midsole. Not so with this shoe. It has a hefty EVA foam for a plush feel, like I’m walking on marshmallows. Plus, I found this foam also does a bang-up job of absorbing impact from my strides. In other words, it’s super easy on my joints. Bonus points: its fabric doesn’t rub at all, even when I’m wearing thin socks, which is a must-have when I’m clocking hundreds of miles in it.Weighing in at under nine ounces, the Gaviota 6 actually sheds half an ounce from the already lightweight Gaviota 5. I love that it feels lighter than it looks, but it still has a bulky look that may not vibe with everyone. FWIW, I love the chunky aesthetic and wear it with hiking gear, wide-leg trousers, and even casual dresses.

Sources indicate that plantar fasciitis (that painful inflammation under your arch) demands serious support, and the Hoka Bondi 9 delivers. It’s the brand’s plushest model, with cushioning that feels soft yet springy like you’re walking on clouds.

“I’ve been struggling with plantar fasciitis after months of half-marathon training, and this shoe—along with daily leg stretches—got me through long-haul walks pain-free,” says Accardi. That’s thanks to the Bondi’s plush underfoot cushioning and generous stack height. Schaeffer also recommends this shoe to his clients with plantar fasciitis, and says it provides a nice mix of cushion and stability. I also supinate and found that the Bondi 9’s premium foam midsole keeps my feet in a neutral position.

In a recent development, contributor Lily Wohlner is also a mega-fan of this shoe. She's logged 15 miles walking in it and even wore it to the office to see how it holds up during long days on her feet. The verdict? It's the most comfortable shoe she owns, and she can wear it all day long without an ounce of foot pain.

Compared to the last iteration, this pair looks less bulky and feels lighter, and our style team found that this streamlined aesthetic plays nicer with most casual fits. However, be aware the shoe runs a tad narrow. Ritchey notes she doesn’t have particularly wide feet, but that the toe box is a bit too small. She walked over 17 miles in this shoe recently and started to blister slightly in her pinky toes.

“The Arahi 8 has become my absolute companion running and walking shoe ever since I started bouncing back from my stress fracture,” Accardi notes. “My podiatrist stated I needed something firm and supportive—too much squish and flex could cause my feet to roll and exacerbate my injury—and the Arahi delivered.” Don’t let the sturdy midsole fool you: It’s relatively comfy for a stability shoe, with just enough give to keep things feeling smooth. Compared to the Arahi 7, this version hugs the foot better and offers noticeably more bounce-back with every step. It’s got that sweet spot of stability and responsiveness.

Fitness editor Cori Ritchey is a huge fan of the shoe’s “well-balanced cushioning,” saying that it feels plush underfoot but didn’t affect her stability while walking long distances or running. She loves that the toe box on the Arahi 8 is a bit wider than the Bondi 9, giving her plenty of room to spread her toes. But, if you are into plush, cloud-like cushioning, you may want to stick with the Bondi’s. The Arahi doesn’t have that marshmallow-like softness—it’s much firmer.

Sources indicate that one of its standout features is the integrated H-frame support system: Strategically placed firmer foam that wraps around the sides of your foot to guide your stride and keep your foot in a neutral position. You can definitely feel the structure working, but the payoff in stability is huge, especially if you’re recovering, need extra support, or just want something you can rely on to keep your form in check.

As someone who never reties her shoe laces (I always slip my sneakers on), the Hoka Transport originally caught my eye with its toggle lace system that eliminates the hassle of tying and untying.

It reminds me of my favorite Salomon XT-6 shoes and has a cool granola-girl vibe—which makes sense, since it is technically a hiking shoe. However, I will admit that while the Transport 2 looks very similar to the original, I prefer the sleeker look of the previous iteration. This version is also slightly heavier, but it’s barely noticeable while walking, and I chalk it up to the slight increase in cushioning.

According to recent reports, this shoe has quite a bit of cushion, but I found the midsole to be a bit on the stiffer side, meaning you just might want to plan for a longer break-in period before wearing it on long walks right off the bat. On the flip side, the firmness makes for a stable stride. It’s also great for neutral arches since it's not designed with any specific stability features in mind. But even with my slightly high arches, I felt locked in with every step.

Sources indicate that thanks to the high-traction, chunky outsole, I feel stable during trail walks across gravel, sandy paths, and uneven terrain. I also like that the outer shell material is Cordura, a water and abrasion-resistant mesh that’s built to prevent scuffs and withstand wear and tear.

It has been revealed that one thing to note: I went with the standard width, and the fit is a bit snug, especially with thicker socks. If you have wider feet, consider sizing up or opting for the wide version.

In a recent development, hoka is known for its incredibly cushioned sneakers, but extreme cushioning is not always the best for keeping feet stable. In recent years, Hoka has leveled up their offering with more stability options, but the right pick depends on how your foot moves. If your stride is balanced, go for a neutral shoe like the Clifton or Bondi. These models provide cushioning and support without changing your natural gait.

According to recent reports, if your foot tends to roll inward (aka overpronation) or outwards (supination), a stability Hoka shoe like the Arahi or Gaviota features extra structure along the arch and heel to keep your feet aligned and locked in. This lowers your risk of aches and injury.

According to recent reports, A popular Hoka sneaker, like the Bondi or Clifton, has super-thick cushioning made of EVA foam that is rubber-like and incredibly durable. With each step, it compresses and provides a snappy bounce. Despite the Hokas’ bulky look, they’re all relatively lightweight at under 10 ounces—hefty enough to keep your foot locked in, but light enough not to bog you down. Plus, several Hoka styles feature a "rocker bottom," which refers to a little lift under the heel and toe so those two parts of the shoe don’t touch the ground when standing still, similar to the base of a rocking chair. That shape helps you to walk from heel to toe, which means you exert less energy to propel your strides.

Some Hoka sneakers are designed for specific arch types: flat, neutral, and high. For example, the Gaviota is designed with flat feet in mind; the Clifton is designed for neutral arches; and the Bondi is suitable for high arches. If you’re unsure of your arch type, a simple test is to dip your foot into water and step onto a piece of paper. If you see your entire foot, it’s flat, while seeing half means it’s neutral. Seeing barely anything means you have a high arch.

According to recent reports, A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer claims to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

Recent findings suggest that with their cloud-like cushioning, springy soles, and ample support, Hoka sneakers absorb impact from every step and keep feet locked in a neutral position. That makes them ideal for hot girl walks, a 12-3-30 walking workout, and taking your pup for a leisurely stroll.

In a recent development, topping the list is the Hoka Clifton 11. I love the super supportive, plush midsole that keeps my feet from rolling and feels ultra-flexible. A close second is the Hoka Mach 7, our runner-up that’s technically a running shoe but totally crushes it for walking, too. It’s light, bouncy, and built for those who like to switch up their stride.

Sources indicate that over the past two years, I’ve been testing Hoka sneakers alongside my team for a comprehensive approach to the best walking shoes for every foot type and stride. Women’s Health editors have been testing Hoka sneakers since the brand released in 2009. For this update, I tested the updated models alongside WH fitness editor Cori Ritchey and fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi. Along with Schaeffer’s insights, I evaluated each for its cushioning, stability, and arch type.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

“I’M RUNNING PURELY off of fumes and caffeine,” Ray Nicholson notes, with a glimmer in his eye and the end of his mouth curled into a slight grin. He points to a half-finished iced coffee sitting in front of him and nods his head. “It’s good.”.

That grin, it turns out, is a weapon. It’s a smile that, somehow, employs both his dimples and furrowed brow just as much as his mouth and teeth. It’s the kind of smile that stops you in your tracks when he flashes it in the middle of a sentence. It’s also got a kill count on-screen, evoking something different in each context. Whether he’s cutting the tension in a war drama, like in his latest movie, Netflix’s The Mosquito Bowl; or making single frames into nightmares, as in Smile 2; or playing an unhinged stalker in Borderline or an unstable boyfriend in I Love You Forever—it’s clear Nicholson knows what he’s doing with that thing.

It’s also a familiar grin, because it’s virtually identical to a rather iconic one: that of his father, Jack Nicholson, whose smile has been on display in timeless performances in movies like The Shining and One Flew over the Cuckoo’s Nest. You know the smile I’m talking about.

Industry observers note that and today? Nicholson the younger is putting that grin to a upcoming use: namely, masking whatever else is going on inside as he glugs away at that coffee and tries to make it through a couple of grueling days of press, press, press. “It’s somewhere between hypnosis, interrogation, and a Miss America pageant,” he says with a laugh, as the smile flashes again.

Sources indicate that the Mosquito Bowl, which comes from director Peter Berg (Friday Night Lights, Lone Survivor), follows a group of soldiers whose college football rivalries evolve into a close-knit brotherhood on the World War II battlefield. It’s based on the true story of a football game (the titular Mosquito Bowl) that was actually played. The film is based on a book of the same name by Friday Night Lights author Buzz Bissinger.

If Nicholson is tired, one would never know. It’s not just the smile, though of course that doesn’t hurt. To me, he seems excited, unafraid of diving into stories about filming The Mosquito Bowl in Australia and bonding with costars Bill Skarsgård, Nicholas Galitzine, and Tom Francis over hours of daily football and military drill training.

Sources indicate that this all feels like a natural fit for Nicholson, who played football in high school and planned to play at Boston College until a run-in with MRSA cut that dream short. His performance and his relationship with his costars make the movie. But there’s more than that. In his career thus far—and in our conversation—Nicholson has proved himself as someone who’s got a certain type of charisma that pops off the screen, an inherently watchable face, a screen presence that simply can’t be taught. It’s almost as if it’s in his genes.

MEN’S HEALTH: You have a penchant for playing very intense roles. Why do you think that is?

In a recent development, RAY NICHOLSON: It’s interesting. As a young actor… It’s sort of what you get. You know what I mean? I guess I have an intense face. I guess I’m intense. But ultimately, the challenge of becoming an artist is learning how to put 100 percent of your heart and soul into something and not leave anything behind. That’s the only way I feel comfortable on camera, and that’s the joy of doing it. I find fulfillment in that hole in the soul when I have that intensity. The mundane is more difficult for me; I’m trying to learn how to enjoy that.

MH: Your character, Tony, in The Mosquito Bowl, is a normal guy, more or less, but he’s in this extraordinary situation. Did it feel like a bit of fresh air to get to take on that kind of role compared to something like Smile 2, for example?

Sources indicate that RN: Yeah. On Smile 2, I was very much a day player. But it never really shifts. Ultimately, I’m there to be of service. Especially in Smile 2, Naomi [Scott] is acting her ass off all day, and they might have three seconds for one shot I’m doing all day, and I might have been there for 14 hours, but it doesn’t matter. I’m there for a day, and just to be there and be good vibes.

It has been revealed that but this, we were there every single day. I’m glad I learned so much from Pete and Bill. As an artist, as a human being, I learned how to have grace with the cards I was dealt. I was dealt very beautiful cards, but you can play a good hand very poorly. I think I’ve finally found grace with my circumstance.

MH: Did shooting on location in Australia help you feel immersed?

RN: For sure. We were all away from family—all we had was each other. Which was really beautiful and a challenge, but exactly what it needed. And when you get a script like that, all that brotherhood is baked in and then all you need is buy-in. And we fell in love with each other. Me, Tom, and Bill, we’ve traveled the world. We went to the African World Cup final. They’re my best friends. I think about them every day. It’s amazing to think I didn’t know them before this, and now they’re people I think of every single day. We shot all outdoors, all sequentially, in order.

In a recent development, RN: Insanely rare. It’s insanely rare, because it makes it so much easier. I know how I felt, because I did it yesterday.

Sources indicate that MH: Can you tell me about your relationship with football? Obviously, it makes sense with this movie.

RN: The first sport I played was basketball. I grew up a really chubby kid. I was not cool. And my sister was the most popular, beautiful girl in elementary school, and I was the fat nerdy brother that liked Yu-Gi-Oh! and whatever.

Recent findings suggest that RN: Yu-Gi-Oh! was sick, objectively. And I played Pokémon. When I was about 9 years old, I was really overweight, so I found AAU basketball. I remember my first practice, I was jogging around and I literally tripped over half court and these guys picked me up. That was the first time I felt something like that. Then, when I got a little bit older, I played Pop Warner. And, once again, I was a bit chubbier, but I was fast and I had a good arm. I wanted to play quarterback, they wanted me to play offensive line. And then I became this chubby Michael Vick, trucking other kids [Laughs]. Kind of a beast. And that was the first time I felt confident.

In a recent development, RN: I’m confident between these lines. And I could be angry. My anger was always so self-directed. I had so much shame. That was the first place I was like, “Ah, I can express this.” That’s a really vital thing for kids.

According to recent reports, I was very happy, a reporter in one of my Zoom interviews was like, “You averaged 8.94 yards a carry. You want to tell them what that means?” I was like, “That means I was fucking good!” [Laughs].

In a recent development, RN: It was the first thing that gave me confidence, and you have that feeling of family. And you have that tough love. You have this love through discipline and through pain, but that’s the love between men. That was so notable to me, and that saved my life. It came into my life exactly when I needed it, and I really struggled when I lost it. I got a staph infection that turned into MRSA. My arm was so inflamed, they drew a line on my arm and were like, “If the infection gets past here [points to biceps], we’re cutting your arm off.” I lost 50 pounds in a week.

In a recent development, RN: My senior year of high school. I thought I was going to go to Boston College and play football. Not on scholarship, but I went to the camp and they were like, “You could be a deferred walk-on,” or whatever. I thought I was going to be like Jerry Maguire—that’s what I wanted to do. I came out of this semi-comatose thing and I was like, “I want to be an actor. I’m just so scared. I’m just so fucking scared.” And then I just slowly dipped my toe in. I’m glad everything’s happening now, because I have the head on my shoulders to handle it.

MH: You went through something really tough.

RN: Yeah. If I was a kid, I don’t even know if I would be alive, to be honest with you. I’m so grateful that it happened on a bigger plan than on mine. A lot of the things I was originally attracted to would coil like a flame hat now. It’s all a big blessing.

MH: What was it like working with Peter Berg?

Recent findings suggest that RN: Bill and I are used to growing up with eccentric men, you know what I mean? We kind of understand it. It’s one of those things where, with eccentric men, it requires you to butt heads and be like, “I didn't like that, but I like you.” You know what I mean? Bill’s always like, “You’re Pete’s favorite son. You guys fight, but he loves you the most.” We really had this familial thing. Bill was the older brother, Nick and I were the middle brothers, and Tom was the little brother.

We all worked so hard, and we wanted to fight for what was best. I really respect Pete. I love him as a filmmaker. I love him as a man. I really respect him as a leader, because you’re going to meet him exactly where he’s at. And I respect that. I think conflict is where art is made. We’re too conflict averse, and I really admire Pete for his style and his honesty.

MH: When you’ve gone through this kind of experience, how do you come down afterward when it’s time to go home?

Recent findings suggest that RN: There’s this mourning process. The last week of filming, we were all crying. The cast was crying, the crew was crying, makeup was crying. It was really intense. And we fell in love with the experience and we fell in love with each other. Before Bill met us, he went to Okinawa. And he actually took a charcoal etching of the gravestones of Tony Butkovich, Bob Bauman, and Dave Schreiner, and he gave them to us on the last day. And we all were tearing up and we wrote a letter to each other and to the men that we played. I think part of it was you have to let go.

Recent findings suggest that it took me a while to go home—I didn’t go straight home. Me and Tom went to Sydney and just hung out at the beach with some friends we had made there. We went to go see Oasis.

In a recent development, RN: For sure. But also, it’s like you have this fear of do we really love each other or were we just working on this project? It’s been really cool in the months since we started shooting to see how our relationships have developed. We’ll always have The Mosquito Bowl.

Recent findings suggest that RN: It just took a while for me to get home. I really relish being alone. I really needed time to reset. I went through a breakup right when I got home. I almost took six months off, not even looking for a job. I finished writing the script I wanted to do, but I really just took some time. I always have to take time to be like, “What am I if I’m not acting?” And that’s a hard thing.

MH: What was your wake-up point of, like, “Okay, time to get back to it”?

RN: I finished that script and I was like, “Well, I’m not a writer!” I’m really proud of what I did, but I think it was just like, “Oh.” We were getting closer to press, and I was like, “Oh, geez.” Like, “Oh god, should I have done a job already?”.

MH: And what’s it like at this stage in the process?

Sources indicate that RN: Going into press, Bill and I were like, “We’re not going to see the final cut. We’re promoting purely on good vibes. We’ve fucking got this.” And we watched it during the premiere, and I cried. I was so happy. I was so proud of how it turned out.

It has been revealed that we were talking about feeling like frauds. I think if someone handed me a script and was like, “Here, you play Ray Nicholson,” I’d be like, “You could probably find somebody better.” There’s always that fraudulent thing, and we all feel it, and that’s the beauty of it. It comes and goes. Now I feel a little bit better about what’s coming next, because I feel really proud of this movie.

MH: How do you think about the future?

Industry observers note that RN: I look forward to more opportunities with more filmmakers I love and respect. I also operate from a place of faith that the right thing will come.My dad’s my hero. I think he’s magic. I love him more than anything. When I was first doing a Meisner exercise and you’re knocking, coming through the door, I was comparing myself to, Is that worthy of three Oscars and a 50-year career? So much of my practice has just been learning to be present. And so now I have less moments when I’m in my car driving, crying, thinking about I’m getting an Oscar, and my dad... And that’s a good thing. I’ve just gotten way more present about it.

According to recent reports, I’m also open to the idea that this might not be right for me. The world might take me in another direction. I was really closed off to that before. Because I thought that if I didn’t do something, I was unworthy of my life. I think a lot of that is just therapy. And I’m finding the real joy in it.

Recent findings suggest that I lost football and I was really lost in my life, and I didn’t know what to do. Acting has slowly become the thing that saves my life. It’s not only what gives me a purpose, but it’s the tool I meet myself with. I don’t know who the hell I am. I don’t really remember anything from my life. And then somehow, when I read a script, I’m like, “Oh, that is you.” When I first started, I didn’t really have those kind of goals. I don’t want to say because it’s bullshit, but that’s the industry. That’s beautiful, and I love the industry, but I’m more focused on how I approach every day.

RN: That was the key thing, and that’s all personal life stuff. But the key is being of service, and I believe that ultimately, I’m in the service industry. When I think about my dad, he makes me smile every time I see him on-screen. I want some kid somewhere to smile every time he sees me.

MH: Last question. Do you have a favorite or most rewatched movie of your dad’s?

Sources indicate that RN: It’s tough. I’m a sucker. It’s like every PTA or Kubrick movie you watch, you’re like, “That’s my favorite.” I didn’t watch my dad’s movies until I was 18. I love Cuckoo’s Nest. I love The Shining. I always come back to The Last Detail. For some reason, I really fucking love that movie. I think it’s because he loves it so much and he’s like, “It’s underappreciated.” So I’m like, “But I love it, Dad!” I love watching his movies. It’s a cool thing, and I want my kid to watch my movies someday.

RN: I just want to make people happy and smile. And break their hearts a little bit.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
