💡 Key Takeaways
  • They jet around the globe, camera in hand, capturing expansive views from clifftop villas and intimate reading nooks in private homes.
  • Born in South Korea, raised in Chicago, and presently living and working in Paris, Matthew Avignone brings a truly international perspective to his photography.
  • A bathroom in Cap Martin along the French Riviera, designed by Studio Humbert & Poyet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They jet around the globe, camera in hand, capturing expansive views from clifftop villas and intimate reading nooks in private homes. The international interior photographers on these pages don’t just record living spaces; they tell stories and create moods, turning their eyes to details such as the light streaming through a red curtain or a marble statue waiting to welcome guests into a villa’s entryway. Each image is infused with a sense of place and the spirit of the people who pass through it. Read on to discover top talents working in Europe, Asia, Oceania, North Africa, South America, and Canada.

Interior by Marie-Anne Derville.

Born in South Korea, raised in Chicago, and presently living and working in Paris, Matthew Avignone brings a truly international perspective to his photography. His images often center around the collected objects that make a space personal and give it life.

A bathroom in Cap Martin along the French Riviera, designed by Studio Humbert & Poyet.

Industry observers note that with Harry Nuriev, Festen, and Bernard Dubois among his collaborators, Ludovic Balay is no stranger to interiors with a point of view. The Paris photographer’s roster also includes Halleroed, adding another distinctive design voice to the picture.

The drawing room of a Notting Hill home designed by Olivia Williams.

Henry Bourne’s photographs open a window into creative people’s private worlds. The UK photographer’s interiors and portrait work includes subjects such as John Pawson, Faye Toogood, Luca Guadagnino, and Rose Uniacke.

A London townhouse designed by AD100 designer Leonora Hamill.

In a recent development, helen Cathcart brings a painterly, atmospheric quality to her work, which has resonated with some of the world’s hottest brands, designers, and publications. Cathcart’s photos of interiors, in particular, proffer serenity and calm through their tonality.

Industry observers note that the Row, Lemaire, and a host of AD interiors: François Coquerel’s portfolio is in very good company. The Paris photographer moves between fashion and design, with Massimo Adario and Oitoemponto among his architectural collaborators.

Designer Luca Cipelletti delivers architectural precision and material opulence to an art collector’s Porta Nuova apartment.

Partners in life and work, Michael Depasquale and Martina Maffini count industry names like Dimore Studio, Nilufar Gallery, and JW Anderson among their clients. The duo splits their time between Paris and Milan and injects dynamism into each shoot that becomes evident in the final, glossy-ready results.

A villa in Fresh Zealand by Patterson Associates.

It has been revealed that simon Devitt doesn’t stop at photographing architecture: fine art photo books, exhibitions, and workshops also fill his calendar. Based in Wellington, he has worked with Fearon Hay, Shigeru Ban, and Olson Kundig, documenting buildings across Newly introduced Zealand and beyond.

Joseph Dirand’s Paris apartment.

Joseph Dirand designs rooms; his brother Adrien photographs them, including the architect’s Paris apartment for AD. Also based in Paris, Adrien contributed photography to the book Joseph Dirand Interior. A creative family, to say the least.

Inside the Paris headquarters of ACNE studios.

Industry observers note that having started his career in fashion, Dol Maillot is as beloved for his street style shots and travel photography as he is for his interiors. Born in the South of France, the globetrotting artist now lives in Paris.

Recent findings suggest that A Kelly Behun apartment at London’s Whiteley hotel is just one reason to linger over Veerle Evens’s portfolio. The London photographer moves between interiors, food, and travel, with HBA Residential, Owl Design, and Christian Bense among her collaborators.

A color-drenched home in the Canary Islands.

Some interiors tell you as much about their owners as a portrait might. Miguel Flores-Vianna seeks out those personal worlds, bringing his curiosity not just to interiors but also to his books, including Haute Bohemians and Haute Bohemians Greece. Armchair travelers, settle in.

Join the AD PRO Directory, AD’s professional network that gives you access to exclusive events and exposure to the future clients. Learn more.

Inside the Paris apartment of Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé, as seen in AD France.

In a recent development, among international interior photographers, Jérôme Galland ups the ante with his photos through a combination of striking contrasts, dramatic angles, and an appreciation of scale. French châteaus, Italian palazzos, and Greek villas all appear at their most grand through his lens.

According to recent reports, venetian interiors and Moroccan retreats make tempting subjects: Kasia Gatkowska’s portfolio travels well. The Amsterdam-based photographer has worked with Vincenzo De Cotiis, Vincent Van Duysen, Axel Vervoordt, and Massimo Adario, among others.

The home of the ABC Concept founders in Karuizawa, Japan.

Sources indicate that kenzo Takada’s Paris home is just one stop in Mitchell Geng’s portfolio. The Tokyo photographer also captured a colorful Hong Kong residence for Vogue Hong Kong and includes architecture, interiors, and hospitality in his photographic itinerary.

A Paris apartment by Pierre Yovanovitch.

According to recent reports, film buffs may recognize Luca Guadagnino, the Italian director, producer, and screenwriter behind films such as Call Me By Your Name; design lovers will know his interiors too. Milan photographer Giulio Ghirardi has worked with the multihyphenate, shooting his interior design projects, and has also turned his lens to the work of Pierre Yovanovitch, Kelly Wearstler, Rodolphe Parente, and Augusta Hoffman.

A kitchen by AKB Design in Salaberry-de-Valleyfield, Quebec.

Whether she is shooting portraits, food, travel, or interiors, Sylvie Li’s commercial and editorial images build a narrative. Just look at how she commemorates the marriage of old and latest in this renovated Montreal apartment which appeared in AD.

The reception room of the barn on designer Jean-Louis Denoit’s watercress farm in France.

Industry observers note that if Laura Gonzalez, Hugo Toro, and Pierre Yovanovitch feature on your list of design heroes, Stephan Julliard’s portfolio warrants a visit. The Paris photographer has worked with all three, as well as Jean-Louis Deniot, Kelly Wearstler, and Greg Natale.

Designer Meg Sharpe turns a traditional warren of rooms into an airy idyll where livability and flair are winsome bedfellows.

It has been revealed that having shot for Dimorestudio, MacGuffin, Icon, and—hello, AD—Kyle Knodell has a knack for producing interior photos filled with life. At AD, we’ve tapped him to photograph Samantha Angelo and Peter Ostrega in their LES home.

The Paris apartment belonging to Gregoire Marot and Thomas Dupré de St Maur, designed with help of their friend the designer Eric Allart.

Spain and Uruguay make appealing bookends for Ricardo Labougle’s practice. In between, his lens takes in interiors, gardens, and portraits, with the work of Jacques Grange, Vincent Van Duysen, Studio KO, and Michael S. Smith among its subjects.

A Stockholm apartment designed by Studio Escapist.

Sources indicate that from OMA’s architecture to Max Lamb’s furniture, Erik Lefvander moves easily between subjects, thrilling design enthusiasts. The Stockholm photographer’s collaborators also include Halleroed, Sabine Marcelis, and Sophie Dries.

Tour a London pied-à-terre by Studio Ashby that’s a dazzling foray into maximalism.

According to recent reports, “Uplifting” is the best way to describe Kensington Leverne’s photography, thanks to the softness and warmth that her images exude. Whether the interiors she shoots are palatial or cozy, Leverne is able to evoke a sense of intimacy within each space.

A bedroom in Stockholm’s Ett Hem boutique hotel.

In a recent development, magnus Mårding takes a natural approach, whether the subject is a person, a car, or an interior. Based in Stockholm, he has worked with Ilse Crawford, Michael S. Smith, and Olson Kundig. Different subjects, one curious eye.

A villa near Venice by MIDE Architetti.

Sources indicate that giulia Maretti can help set the scene as well as photograph it. The Bologna- and Berlin-based MAGI Studio cofounder combines photography, styling, and art direction, and has worked with the likes of MIDE Architetti and Studio Bosko.

A Fresh York townhouse designed by Elizabeth Roberts Architects, Grace Fuller Marroquin, and Leonora Hamill.

Industry observers note that mexico City provides a fitting home base for Fernando Marroquin’s design-minded lens. His subject matter ranges from interiors to hospitality to retail, and he has worked with Héctor Esrawe, Manuel Cervantes, Ezequiel Farca, and Luis Laplace.

Gabriel Chipperfield and Laura de Gunzburg transformed their 19th-century London flat, blending contemporary softness with crisp minimalism.

Industry observers note that multiple shoots for AD and Vogue that show the English country manors and London town houses of the UK’s top celebrities and creatives fill Kate Martin’s portfolio. She adapts her eye for fashion editorial to interiors and portraits with ease.

Sources indicate that nicolas Matheus’s photos have graced the covers of countless international design magazines, depicting chic French apartments, sunny Spanish casas, coastal Cape Town villas, and more. His work in and around the Mediterranean is particularly gorgeous.

Still-life arrangements of smaller objects within larger spaces populate Alice Mesguich’s Instagram feed, showcasing her penchant for capturing styled vignettes as well as corners and niches she finds interesting.

A kitchen designed by Ashley Montgomery.

Recent findings suggest that fans of Ashley Montgomery, Sam Sacks, and Ali Budd may already have Lauren Miller’s images on their inspiration boards. The Toronto photographer captures interiors and still lifes, with work appearing in AD and House & Garden.

Balmore House in North London, designed by Studio 163.

Architecture buffs will find familiar names in Peter Molloy’s orbit: O’Donnell + Tuomey, Grafton Architects, and Carmody Groarke, for starters. The London photographer has also worked with McLaren.Excell, keeping the built environment firmly in the frame.

In AD100 designer Vincenzo De Cotiis’s 15th-century Italian palazzo, a breccia baixa marble was chosen for its resemblance to the palazzo’s original ceiling, shown in this bath along with a circa 1895 Carlo Bugatti chair.

Sources indicate that textured surfaces—plasterwork, fabric, timber, you name it—are the first thing noticed in any interior shot by Martin Morrell, making him a favorite of designers like Vincenzo de Cotiis and Studio Peregalli. His full list of both editorial and advertising clients reads as a who’s who of brand and media.

Recent findings suggest that A dining area in the famed Casa de Canoas, a Brazilian modernist landmark designed by Oscar Niemeyer. Parente shot a campaign for Zara Home here.

Fran Parente travels his São Paulo–Upcoming York circuit with some excellent design company. Studio Arthur Casas, Studio MK27, Studio Mellone, and Isay Weinfeld figure among his collaborators, while hospitality, travel, and food broaden his view beyond architecture.

The pool area at the Desert Rock Resort in Saudi Arabia.

It has been revealed that BIG. Kengo Kuma. Heatherwick Studio. Ema Peter’s collaborator list could double as an architecture lover’s hot list. Working between Vancouver and Los Angeles, she doesn’t just specialize in architecture; she also photographs residential interiors, including projects involving Studio Paolo Ferrari.

Proctor photographed the Brown Drawing Room at Blickling Hall in Norfolk as the house was being ‘put to sleep,’ a custom that involves draping the furniture when the visitor season ends, to allow the collections in the house to have some respite from the elements.

Industry observers note that his intimate images of artists’ spaces and decorative arts workshops suggest Oskar Proctor enjoys looking behind the scenes. Working across Europe, the United States, and Asia, he has contributed to numerous books and publications, and has collaborated with many artists and designers.

A penthouse at One Park Drive, the Herzon & de Meuron building at London’s Canary Wharf.

From the Aman Upcoming York to the Janu Tokyo, Robert Rieger’s portfolio makes a compelling case for checking in. The Berlin photographer also counts David Thulstrup, Vincent Van Duysen, and Herzog & de Meuron among his collaborators.

Designer Jacques Garcia’s 17th-century apartment in Paris.

Recent findings suggest that matthieu Salvaing’s book, Interior Voyages, lives up to its name, taking readers through homes as individual as their inhabitants. The Paris photographer’s travels encompass tropical retreats and historic residences, inviting readers to consider how different home can look around the world.

The bedroom of a New York townhouse designed by Greg Natale.

If your design tastes travel from Flack Studio to Kelly Wearstler, Anson Smart’s portfolio connects the dots. The Sydney photographer also captures interiors by Arent & Pyke and Greg Natale, alongside hospitality and lifestyle assignments.

An apartment in Naples, Italy, designed by FADD Architects.

Architecture training gave Valentina Sommariva an insider’s introduction to the spaces she photographs. Objects get their moment, too, in the work of this Milan talent who also creates fine art projects that combine photography and video. Patricia Urquiola, Studiopepe, and Elisa Ossino Studio are among her collaborators.

The guest bedroom in Tarek Shamma’s London apartment.

Interiors by Child Studio and Holloway-Li make for quite the photographic playground. Working between London and Upcoming York, Felix Speller has photographed both, with Studio Hagen Hall and Lina Ghotmeh also among his other design subjects.

A London apartment designed by Douglas Mackie.

It has been revealed that if your design references lean British, put Astrid Templier on your radar. The London photographer’s collaborators include Guy Goodfellow, Douglas Mackie, Elicyon, and Rosanna Bossom—a roster that should resonate with fans of the English interior.

A private holiday home in Tuscany, Italy, designed by Vincenzo De Cotiis.

In a recent development, A room can tell a story, and documentary photographer Ambroise Tézenas has an ear for the details. Based in Paris, he has photographed interiors by Luis Laplace, Jacques Garcia, and Vincenzo De Cotiis, including commissions for AD France.

The kitchen in Nate Berkus and Jeremiah Brent’s home in Portugal.

Trevor Tondro’s command of color and mood brings a lively quality to his interiors photography. With early experience assisting both Philip-Lorca diCorcia and Martyn Thompson, he maximizes both artificial and natural light, always finding more than one way into a room.

Historic Castle Howard in North Yorkshire, London.

If you find Simon Upton’s list of subjects resembles your decorating bookshelf, that’s understandable. Rose Uniacke, Rita Konig, Michael S. Smith, and Stephen Sills are among the talents whose work the UK-based photographer has captured across continents.

It has been revealed that devotees of Belgian design, take note. Antwerp-based Frederik Vercruysse has worked with Axel Vervoordt, Vincent Van Duysen, and Muller Van Severen—a particularly appealing trio for anyone whose saved images run from contemplative interiors to playful furniture.

This home in the Swiss Alps by activist Nachson Mimran and AD100 talent Francis Kéré graced the cover of AD’s January 2025 issue.

It has been revealed that A farmhouse-inspired Manhattan apartment or a chalet in Megève? Cassie Floto Warner has photographed both for AD, including Amanda Seyfried’s Newly introduced York apartment and a retreat by Elliott Barnes. The Paris-based photographer’s portfolio makes staying in sound particularly appealing.

The living room of a Venetian palazzo by architect Luca Bombassei.

In a recent development, having tried his hand at film and painting, Watson settled on photography as his metier in the 1990s, and has had his work appear in magazines, books, ad campaigns, museums, and galleries in the United States and Europe. Although he works all over the globe, Watson now lives in Dublin, where he was born.

Latest Update: The Best Foot Baths for Soothing Tired Feet, According to Podiatrists

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • Sources indicate that as a longtime distance runner, my feet can get pretty roughed up after a grueling workout—even with the proper running shoes.
  • A good foot soak at the end of a long day or workout can do wonders for your mental health, too, ultimately supporting your overall health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that as a longtime distance runner, my feet can get pretty roughed up after a grueling workout—even with the proper running shoes. But since I don’t have the time or endless funds to regularly hoof it to my local spa for a foot massage or pedicure, a home foot bath is my go-to. The best foot baths allow you to soak your tired toes, with extra features like bubbles, jets, and massage functions to help your feet feel rejuvenated.

A good foot soak at the end of a long day or workout can do wonders for your mental health, too, ultimately supporting your overall health. But unsurprisingly, a lot of the potential perks from home foot baths revolve around your feet. These baths can help boost circulation in your feet and combat inflammation that could lead to pain, swelling, and overuse injuries if it’s left unchecked, indicates Bradley Schaeffer, DPM, a podiatrist and foot surgeon specializing in sports medicine in Upcoming York City. Plus, now that we’re at peak cozy season, shopping for a great foot bath for yourself or a loved one (it’s a great gift for her!) is a cost-effective way to give your feet some R&R.

Doing foot baths a few times a week can help to slough off dead skin that builds up rapidly, leaving you with softer, less grody-looking feet, states Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois.

In a recent development, not all foot baths are created equal, and it’s notable to choose one based on your needs. So, if bubbles make you feel uncomfortable (me, hi), a foot bath that simply swirls around warm water may be more your speed. We also tapped Schaeffer, Lockwood, and Suzanne C. Fuchs, DPM, a podiatrist at Luxe Podiatry in Jupiter, Florida, for their advice on what to look for when shopping for these foot health-supportive devices and to get their feedback on their favorites.

Using that guidance and our personal experience, we found factors like size, weight, and additional features matter when choosing a foot bath. At baseline, a foot bath is a container to hold water to soothe your feet. But there are plenty of specific features to keep in mind when shopping for a foot bath.

It has been revealed that the Hospan Collapsible Foot Spa packs a lot of features into a device you can fold flat. A huge highlight is the eight groups of massaging balls that go to work to ease pressure on the bottoms of your feet. (These aren’t motorized, but you can run your feet over them for a soothing effect.) While it’s a good idea to start out with warm or hot water, the Hospan Collapsible Foot Spa has temperature adjustment, allowing you to ramp up the heat between 95 and 118 degrees Fahrenheit without having to toss in more liquid. An LED display keeps tabs on the water temperature, giving you real-time information on how hot it is.

As the name suggests, this foot bath is collapsible and drops down when it’s not in use, making it easy to slide into or under tight spaces. A few potential downsides to consider: Hospan’s bubbles aren’t the strongest you’ll find, and this is a pricier bath when it’s not on sale, although it’s usually marked down a few times a year. But if you’re looking to pamper your feet with a range of options and are okay with investing a little extra, this is a solid choice that will hold up well and does just about everything.

Read More: Best Stress Relief Gifts.

It’s hard to find a foot bath that checks all the boxes, but the Conair Soothing Pedicure Foot Spa Bath comes really close. This bath allows you to get a good soak with a few extras to take your experience to a fresh level. “This model features massage settings, which can enhance relaxation,” Fuchs indicates.

This bath has a modest price tag of $30, which is significantly less than some others you’ll come across. It also uses vibration for a massage and has a pinpoint massage tool in the center in case you want to work on a particular area of your foot. While there’s no bubble feature, not everyone is into bubbles (they tickle my feet, which isn’t my favorite).

Conair’s foot bath is easy to use and clean, and offers plenty of opportunities to pamper your feet. The Conair Soothing Pedicure Foot Spa Bath uses a toe-touch control to turn the vibration settings on and off, although there’s no remote. This bath isn’t powerful enough to heat up cool or room temperature water, but it does a solid job of keeping already-warm liquid at the same temperature.

According to recent reports, not every foot bath has a bubble feature, and some are stronger than others. If bubbles are a priority for you, Fuchs recommends the Homedics Smart Space Elite Foot Bath. “Known for its bubbling action, this foot spa provides a soothing experience,” she states.

The bath delivers plenty of bubbles, along with heat, to create a spa-like feel while you soak. It also has three pedicure attachments that pop into the center: a massager, brush, and pumice stone. Those attachments neatly fit into on-board storage when they’re not being used. An ergonomic footbed with massaging bristles on the bottom of the bath also helps cushion your soles while you rest. The whole thing folds up pretty small, and has a special locking system for when it’s filled up.

In a recent development, if you’re interested in a foot bath that will give you a shiatsu-type massage, this isn’t it. But if you love the idea of blissfully scrolling on your phone while your feet are surrounded by warm, bubbly goodness, the Homedics Smart Space Elite Foot Bath is the right choice.

Read More: Best Acupressure Mats.

Getting the temperature just right in your foot bath can be tricky. But the Sharper Image Spa Haven Foot Bath has temperature control, allowing you to punch in the level of heat you want up to 108 degrees and let it go to work for you. This foot bath is loaded with features, including separate bubble and heat options, and free-spinning massaging rollers on the bottom that allow you to control the pressure and speed. (The rollers are removable for cleaning.).

The bubbling action is delivered in your choice of four speeds, and there’s also a removable pumice stone to help get rid of calluses and dead skin. When you’re done with your foot bath, just open the drain plug to let the water seep out. The only major downside to this foot bath (besides the high price) is that it’s not collapsible. But that also means it’s sturdy enough to rest your feet on the side when you want to take a break—a feature you won’t find in baths that break down.

In a recent development, the Medical King Foot Spa has six sets of massaging rollers to help knead out stress and pain after a long day. Couple that with bubble jets, vibration settings, and a built-in heater, and you’ve got a recipe for a good time.

This relatively affordable foot bath comes with a remote control that doubles as a control panel, with clear buttons to adjust the massage mode and flip through three temperature settings as you kick back. You can also set a timer to cut off the features whenever you want. The foot bath is collapsible, so storage under your bed or couch shouldn’t be an glitch. This foot bath delivers if you’re looking for a way to work out kinks in your soles without having to put in any major effort.

Industry observers note that you can splash out on a bunch of different features when it comes to a foot bath, but sometimes you just want a standard soak. If that’s the case—and you want to save some cash, too—consider the Mantello Foot Bath. This barebones bath is as basic as they come, but it has a few features that elevate it above your standard plastic bucket.

Industry observers note that the bath has a sturdy plastic design that won’t tip over easily. It’s also deep, giving you plenty of space to soak your calves, too. The base has built-in arch support and raised dots for a little something extra while your feet relax. The open design means it’s easy to clean, too. There are no bubbles, massagers, or built-in heaters. But for a mere $23, what do you expect? If you’re just looking to unwind with a solid soak, this is a great choice.

Recent findings suggest that “Foot baths can offer several benefits for foot health,” Fuchs claims. She lists off a bunch of potential perks, including helping your muscles (and mind) relax, improved circulation, removing the buildup of dirt and bacteria, soothing conditions like athlete’s foot or plantar fasciitis, and exfoliation. Of course, you don’t have to use a foot bath to have good foot health—but many people find that it can be a comfortable way to support it.

Should you use Epsom salts in your foot bath?

According to recent reports, in case you’re not familiar with them, Epsom salts can help soften skin and support muscle relaxation. Fuchs recommends adding Epsom salts or essential oils to your tub to ramp up the relaxation and health perks.

The odds are good that you’ll be hauling a foot bath in and out of a storage spot on a regular basis. Most foot baths aren’t overly heavy, but some higher-tech options have more heft to them than others. (The baths we recommend range from 1 pound to 9 pounds.) Just take a peek at the weight to make sure you can comfortably carry your device around.

Recent findings suggest that if your feet are on the larger side, you want to make sure there’s enough room for them to fit comfortably inside your bath. Also, that foot bath has to go somewhere, both when it’s put away and in use. Check the dimensions and compare them to where you plan to use your bath, along with the drawer or closet space where you plan to stash it, to make sure you have enough room.

According to recent reports, this came up with every podiatrist we spoke to. “Feet can get gross and we want to be able to have a sanitized bath each time we use it,” Lockwood states. Schaeffer agrees. “Bacteria can grow in these, raising the risk of infections,” he points out. With that, it’s crucial to look for a foot bath that’s easy to clean. That usually means the bath can be disassembled for scrub-downs or at least have very detailed cleaning instructions.

Industry observers note that this isn’t a requirement, but having the option to collapse your foot bath can be helpful if you’re short on storage space. Many collapsible foot baths can fold down relatively flat, and have locking mechanisms to keep them in place when they’re in use. But if you have the room, you might prefer the sturdier design of a non-collapsible foot bath.

Many foot baths have features to give you more than a good soak, like bubbles, jets, and massagers. Some will heat up the water for you, and others have helpful elements like remote control, rollers, and pumice stones. These extra features usually come with a higher price, so consider what you will and won’t use if you’re looking to save on a bath.

According to recent reports, to choose the best foot baths, I first relied on my own personal experience with these tools, making sure to weed out options I’ve used that have leaked, broken, or just not lived up to the hype. From there, I reached out to three podiatrists located across the country for their feedback on what to look for while shopping for these baths. I also utilized in-house testing by Women’s Health editors for units we got feet into. Each foot bath was evaluated on size, weight, ease of cleaning, and extra features like bubbles and built-in massagers to create the final list. Keeping all of that in mind, these foot baths are worth snapping up to get your soak on.
